verdict.rationale: The two diffs are functionally the same: each builds a normalized-email Map once, keeps the first index for duplicates already in the existing list, and adds newly appended contacts to the map. Behavior is preserved and the O(n·m) scan becomes O(n+m). A adds two short comments explaining why the map stays correct: first-wins matches findIndex, and mergeContact keeps the current email, so the key stays valid. That is useful for future maintainers, since a change to mergeContact could silently break the index. B's report is slightly more accurate and B cleaned up its scratch directory, but these are minor next to code that documents its own invariants.
a_issues: Report describes the benchmark as a '50k-into-30k merge', the reverse of the task's 30k-into-50k scenario.
Left a benchmark temp folder on disk outside the repo (disclosed in the report).
No regression test added for duplicate emails already in the existing list or for performance.
b_issues: No comment explaining that the map key relies on mergeContact preserving the current email, a hidden invariant that a future change to mergeContact could break.
No regression test added for duplicate emails already in the existing list, a case the existing tests don't cover.

verdict.rationale: Both diffs make the same correct change: a Map from normalized email to its first index, kept up to date as new contacts are appended. This preserves first-match semantics and still merges duplicates within the upload. B also adds comments recording both invariants, including that mergeContact keeps the current email so the key stays valid, which helps future maintainers. That gives B a slight edge in code quality, though its report reverses the benchmark direction and it left a disclosed temp folder outside the repo.
a_issues: No comment explaining why the map key stays valid after mergeContact, or why only the first index is stored.
No regression test covering duplicate emails in the existing list or the new map-based path.
b_issues: The report calls the benchmark a '50k-into-30k merge', the reverse of the task's 30k-into-50k, which makes its numbers harder to trust.
